rv.q: The best thing about this play is that it’s positioned precisely at this intersection of comedy and pain.
Lane as the tortured soul at the play's heart is magnificent -- showing sides that are charming, witty, savage, self-destructive and yearning.
It shows you the real pain of a real man, and makes you feel what he feels.
Nathan Lane gives a performance of such depth and humanity that it transforms what could have been a standard backstage weepie into something genuinely moving.
The Nance may turn out to be its dramatic high point.
Lane, in the apotheosis of his sad clown routine, is sensational throughout.
Nathan Lane gives a powerhouse performance in Douglas Carter Beane's moving drama
With his hunger to entertain and his precision timing, Lane reminds us why he’s a vaudevillian master in those scenes.

So even when material lets him down, which it finally does in 'The Nance,' Douglas Carter Beane's splendidly ambitious but psychologically superficial tragicomedy, it's thrilling to watch Lane bond with a character who demands the full attention of so many gifted layers of him.

Though they have a sexual and political specificity that would have been verboten in the 1930s, they also bring to mind the clichés of showbiz soaps from that era, in which alcohol, temperament and self-hatred drive a talented star to the skids.
Douglas Carter Beane has written a play that's both hilarious and heartbreaking, examining the cost of hiding one's true self in a world that demands conformity.
What’s amazing about this scene is Lane is hilariously funny while he breaks our hearts.
After a steady diet of Broadway plays that are all about dysfunctional and sitcom-style families, 'The Nance' is a welcome departure.
It also allows Lane to combine his comedic persona with a tragic undertone, not unlike his fine performance in the 2009 revival of “Waiting for Godot.”
Like Chauncy's two worlds, Beane's eventually crumble as well.
Lane reaffirms his status as one of the stage's brightest treasures.
Lane's three-dimensional portrait of Chauncey Miles -- named after George Chauncey, whose 1994. Gay New York Beane consulted for background info -- is never a let-down.
I spent most of “The Nance” fascinated by the subject matter but frustrated by Beane’s execution.
Beyond that, things get a little murky.
A thoughtful and compassionate study in the forgotten ways of the metropolitan world of the last century, 'The Nance' is a flawed yet rich play that offers a great deal of heartbreak and hilarity.

cn.t: Lane delivers a powerhouse performance in Beane's ambitious but uneven period drama about a burlesque comic in 1930s New York. Critics praise the acting and production values while noting the play doesn't fully coalesce.

sg.ra: Center orchestra rows D-G offer head-on sightlines to the high stage without neck strain. Gentle rake; intimate 922-seat house means even mid-orchestra feels close. Playbill notes Oh, Mary! action is downstage center, rewarding central seats.

Telecharge lists extreme sides of the first 11 orchestra rows as obstructed-view seats per Playbill. SeatPlan confirms double-digit seats are angled with far-side stage obstruction. 1903 house geometry leaves sharp side angles near stage.

sg.n: Orchestra Rear (Rows L-O, behind mezz overhang)
sg.ra: TickPick and SeatPlan both confirm Mezzanine overhang begins at Row L of Orchestra. AVFMS reviewer for O12 praised tiered rake ('raised above the row in front so you don't have any heads blocking you'). Fine for plays; top-of-stage cutoff limits tall-set musicals.

SeatPlan: 'patrons can look directly down to the stage, taking advantage of the Mezzanine's fantastic aerial views which don't sacrifice detail.' Excellent rake prevents blocked views. Ideal for spectacle/musicals where staging composition matters.

Folliesbroadway and Headout both flag Mezz D-F center as best value: clean sightlines, excellent rake, priced materially below front-mezz/prime-orchestra. Balcony overhang doesn't cut in until Row C so D-F also sit past the cutoff line without being affected (SeatPlan note is about row C).

sg.n: Mezzanine Rear (behind Row C — balcony overhang) and Side Double-Digits
sg.ra: SeatPlan: 'Balcony overhang kicks in at row C, so views behind this may experience cut-off at the top of the stage.' Double-digit side seats (D24, G22) have partial sightlines. Fine for plays; poor for tall scenic musicals.

Rows B and C clear the Row A safety rail and preserve a steep but clean center view. Tripadvisor: 'Great view of the stage, although a bit of an angled view down.' Starting prices on SeatPlan as low as $68-$80. Steep rake is uncomfortable but preserves sightlines.

sg.n: Balcony Row A and Side L/R front rows
sg.ra: Row A front has a safety rail that cuts across the stage (SeatPlan, Playbill, Tripadvisor all independently confirm). TickPick: Balcony L and R first two rows have partial views due to railing. Shorter patrons especially affected.
